bp: A medical question-answering system is often used when a person has worry but not enough vocabulary to ask a precise clinical question. The dangerous moment is not only when the model knows too little medicine; it is when the user's question itself can mean several different things. A query like a symptom description may omit age, duration, medication, pregnancy status, severity, or prior conditions. If the system chooses one interpretation and answers confidently, it can give advice for the wrong situation. This paper treats that missing specificity as the central safety problem. Its real-world goal is to make a medical large language model notice when the question has not pinned down one answerable case. Instead of always answering, the system should sometimes pause and ask for clarification. That changes medical QA from a one-shot answer machine into a safer conversation gate: answer when the input is clear enough, and request missing details when the uncertainty comes from the user's words.
wh: The hard part is that ambiguous questions can still look fluent and medically relevant. A large language model can usually produce a plausible answer because language contains many common patterns. That fluency hides the fact that several patient situations may fit the same surface text. The paper links this to aleatoric uncertainty, meaning uncertainty that cannot be removed by making the model smarter because the input itself leaves facts unspecified. This differs from ordinary model ignorance. If the question lacks crucial context, reading the question again or running the same model more times does not create the missing fact. Existing uncertainty estimates can also be costly if they require multiple model passes, or invasive if they require changing the whole model through fine-tuning. In a medical setting, the system needs a cheap, early warning that the input is under-specified before it commits to advice. The tension is safety versus speed: asking clarification too often frustrates users, but answering ambiguous questions can reduce accuracy in high-stakes care.
naive: A smart beginner would ask the medical model to answer every user question and maybe include a cautious disclaimer. If the answer sounds uncertain, the system could add "consult a doctor" or sample several responses and compare them. This fails because the model may sound certain about one hidden interpretation while ignoring others. Multiple runs may also be expensive and still circle around the same missing detail. Another beginner move is to hand-write rules: ask follow-up questions whenever certain symptom words appear. That breaks because ambiguity is not tied to a fixed word list. The same word can be clear in one sentence and vague in another. The paper instead looks for ambiguity inside the model's own processing of the question.
ap: The core idea is to detect the kind of uncertainty caused by an under-specified question before generating a final medical answer. The authors first build CV-MedBench, a benchmark made for studying input ambiguity in medical QA. They then examine the model's internal activation patterns, which are the intermediate numerical signals the model produces while reading the query. The key finding reported in the abstract is that aleatoric uncertainty is linearly encoded there: in plain terms, a simple separating direction in those internal signals can mark when a question looks ambiguous. AU-Probe uses that direction as a lightweight detector. It does not fine-tune the whole large language model and does not need several forward passes. The surrounding Clarify-Before-Answer process uses the detector as a gate. If the probe sees high input ambiguity, the system asks the user to clarify; if not, it proceeds to answer.
mech: The mechanism begins with one user query for medical question answering. The query is fed into an open large language model, which reads it and forms hidden states: internal numeric summaries produced at intermediate layers while the model processes the words. The paper's analysis says that these hidden states contain a usable signal about input ambiguity. AU-Probe is attached as a small module that reads those states directly. Its job is not to produce the medical answer. Its job is to score whether the uncertainty comes from the question being under-specified. Because the signal is described as linearly encoded, the probe can behave like a simple measuring ruler over the hidden-state pattern: on one side are questions whose wording points to a sufficiently clear answer; on the other side are questions where several interpretations remain live. The Clarify-Before-Answer process then branches. For low detected ambiguity, the system allows the normal QA path to continue. For high detected ambiguity, it proactively requests missing information from the user before answering. CV-MedBench supplies the controlled setting for building and evaluating this behavior around ambiguous medical questions. The reported experiments compare this gate against baselines across four open models and measure whether adding clarification improves answer accuracy.
math: The main mathematical idea is uncertainty measurement. Probability is the language for acting when a system cannot see the full situation, but this paper cares about a special kind of uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty means the remaining possibilities are caused by the input itself. If a medical question leaves out key facts, there may be no single correct answer until the user supplies them. The second idea is representation engineering, which means inspecting the model's internal numerical summaries rather than only its final words. A hidden state is a compressed record of what the model has made of the question so far. The paper reports that ambiguity is linearly encoded in those records. Linear here means the detector can use a simple weighted sum of internal signals, like drawing a straight boundary through a cloud of cases, to separate more ambiguous from less ambiguous inputs. That matters because a simple boundary is cheaper than repeatedly asking the whole model to answer. The third idea is decision gating: turn an uncertainty score into an action, either answer or clarify. The tradeoff is false confidence versus unnecessary interruption. The math is useful only if the hidden-state signal truly tracks under-specification, not merely topic difficulty or scary medical language.
dots: This paper sits in the conference's probability and information thread because it asks where uncertainty lives and how a system should spend effort when uncertainty is high. It is close to language-model safety work in the repo that treats fluent answers as insufficient when evidence, privacy, or user context is fragile. It also connects to tool-use and agent papers, even though it is medical QA rather than tool retrieval, because the model is given a gate before action: decide whether to continue or ask for more input. The broader pattern is controlled attention under uncertainty. Search systems ask for better query intent, retrieval systems fetch more evidence when internal confidence is weak, and recommendation or moderation systems route hard cases to stronger checks. This paper applies the same shape to healthcare language. Its specific contribution is narrowing the uncertainty source: not all uncertainty means the model lacks knowledge; sometimes the user's question has not yet defined the patient situation.
ww: The approach should help because it intervenes before the model converts ambiguity into a polished answer. A naive system treats the user's words as enough and lets the model choose an interpretation silently. AU-Probe tries to catch the earlier internal sign that the words still support multiple meanings. If that sign is reliable, asking a clarification changes the input itself, which is exactly the right repair for aleatoric uncertainty. More training data or a larger model cannot infer a fact the user never provided, but a follow-up question can bring that fact into the conversation. The lightweight design also matters. A safety check that requires several full model calls may be too slow or costly for routine QA, and fine-tuning every medical model creates deployment friction. Reading hidden states in one pass gives the system a cheap chance to stop unsafe answering. The reported 9.48 percent average accuracy gain over baselines across four open models supports the claim that clarifying ambiguous input improves the downstream answers, not just the uncertainty score.
po: The payoff is a safer medical QA pattern: the system can proactively ask for missing details instead of giving a confident answer to an unclear question. The abstract reports CV-MedBench as a benchmark for studying medical input ambiguity, a lightweight AU-Probe that works from hidden states without fine-tuning or multiple forward passes, and experiments across four open large language models. The measured benefit is an average 9.48 percent accuracy improvement over baselines. In practical terms, the paper buys a fast ambiguity alarm and a clear action tied to it: clarify before answering when the query is under-specified.
limits: The claims depend on CV-MedBench representing the kinds of ambiguity real users bring to medical QA. If real patients omit different facts, mix symptoms differently, or write in styles not covered by the benchmark, the probe may misread ambiguity. The abstract says ambiguity is linearly encoded in internal activation patterns, but it does not specify which layers, medical domains, languages, or patient groups were tested. A clarification gate also needs a good follow-up question; detecting ambiguity is not the same as knowing the safest detail to ask for. The reported experiments use four open models, so transfer to closed, larger, or clinically deployed systems is not proven here.
